content:
Earlier this year, I swapped out a battery-powered push mower for a robot mower that can be controlled from an iPhone. That model builds a virtual map by having you manually drive it along the edges of your yard. Once set up, it clips the grass on a schedule automatically.

Recently, I've been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It takes a very different approach to navigation, and after several weeks of testing, I think for many people it may simply be the easier choice.

Camera-driven automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier comes down to how each robot understands your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses RTK base-station positioning, which during setup required me to manually drive the mower from my iPhone along the boundary once to build an initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, by contrast, uses what the company calls TerraVision 2.0. With three cameras, the mower can automatically map out and navigate the lawn without any buried boundary wire or a separate RTK antenna.

The automatic initial mapping is indeed slower, but I think it may be easier for someone who isn't quite as keen on wrestling with technology.

To test that idea, I had my mum, who lives in another state, set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own, without any help from me at all. She said it worked well for her. I'm not so sure she would have had the patience to manually drive a robot around the entire boundary and then mark off each area to avoid.

Automatic mapping did introduce one small quirk in my front yard. There's no fence or physical divider between my lawn and my neighbour's, so the TerraMow initially included some of their turf in my map.

I solved it by marking that area as a no-go zone in the app. Still, for lawns without a clear visible boundary, it is something to watch out for during the initial mapping process.

A view from the mower's cameras

The cameras on the TerraMow also support one of my favourite features. The iPhone app lets you watch a live feed of what the mower sees as it works.

While testing, I used iPhone Mirroring on my Mac to open that feed in a big window. I could sit comfortably indoors and watch the mower move around the backyard from the mower's own perspective.

It's not strictly necessary for automatic mowing, but beyond making the robot more fun to watch, it also helps explain from time to time why it slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 does not offer a similar camera view.

The two iPhone apps are similar in many ways, letting you schedule work times, adjust mowing settings, create zones, mark areas to avoid, and control the mower remotely.

TerraMow has a rather thoughtful twist on this last feature. Beyond the usual left- and right-thumb virtual joysticks, the app offers a single-handed joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone naturally and steer the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower from an iPhone isn't the primary use of either system; ideally, the robot runs on its schedule without intervention. That said, TerraMow's joystick control is very handy for going back over patches the robot missed.

It sometimes almost felt like I was controlling the robot with telekinesis (the good kind). I could hold the iPhone down at my side while walking, and steer the mower with barely a flick of my thumb.

Every robot mower app should copy this control scheme.

More aggressive mowing

The TerraMow V1000 also feels more aggressive overall than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was louder at work.

I wouldn't call the TerraMow noisy, but the difference is audible. The Anthbot runs so quietly that it's easy to forget it's working, even when it's out there mowing after dark with its headlights on.

Because TerraMow relies on its cameras to navigate, it needs daylight to work reliably, so it matters more to schedule it during the day.

The V1000 also feels solid and is larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage that covers the charging dock, while the Anthbot's garage is a separate purchase.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has been consistently steady. I used it for several weeks in a row, and never had to step in and handle the mowing myself.

When adaptive mapping gets too clever

The same visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes work against it.

The mower continually adjusts its map based on what it sees. Saving those adjustments after each mow takes a fairly long time, during which you can't do anything else in the app.

After several days of rain in a row, I ran into an interesting edge case. A section of the lawn had standing water, and TerraMow reasonably avoided that area on its next run.

Inside the circular patch it skipped, the grass grew taller than the grass around it. Over time, the mower seemed to treat that taller patch as something to keep avoiding, and the area stayed uncut long after the ground had dried out.

I eventually solved it by using the app's remote control to manually drive the mower through the tall grass. Once that area looked like normal lawn again, automatic mowing resumed as usual.

Trimming the edges regularly also helps TerraMow reach the boundary reliably. If the grass near the boundary grows tall, it can otherwise be mistaken for an obstacle rather than part of the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive by comparison. It leans more on the boundaries and obstacles you set up yourself, so there's more upfront work, but it avoids the map "changing its mind" about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac review

After using both systems, I think TerraMow's camera-based approach is the better fit for most people.

For me, burying boundary wire is a non-starter from the start, and setting up an RTK base station means one more piece of hardware to place, power, and maintain. TerraMow avoids both of those requirements.

Its visual navigation isn't flawless: initial mapping takes longer, an invisible property line needs a manual fix, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook a patch of tall grass for a permanent obstacle.

All of those issues are manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable automatic mowing, an entertaining live camera feed, and the best manual controls I've used in a robot mower app.

I genuinely enjoy working in the yard, but mowing is the repetitive, boring part. With a robot handling it, I can focus on landscaping, trimming the edges, and the detail work, while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 delivers on that front and earns my recommendation, especially for anyone looking to avoid burying wire, setting up an RTK antenna, or manually driving a robot around the entire yard from an iPhone.

Amazon currently lists the TerraMow V1000 at US$999, and the site offers a US$200 coupon that can bring the price down further. It's also available to purchase directly from TerraMow's official website.
